title: Drafts, Not Decisions: Why My AI Tools Never Act Alone
linkedin_md:
# Drafts, Not Decisions: Why My AI Tools Never Act Alone

You're building an LLM system that needs to work in the real world. The pressure is to automate, to remove the human from the loop, to chase the vision of a fully autonomous agent. I push back. My core design principle: AI generates drafts. Humans make decisions.

The fastest way to lose user trust, stakeholder buy-in, or even create a real-world mess, is an autonomous mistake. A system that confidently does the wrong thing is worse than a system that asks for help. The draft-only model isn't a limitation. It's a forcing function for reliability, safety, and iterative improvement.

## The Trust Equation

Trust in software is built on predictability and corrigibility. When an AI makes a decision, you surrender a degree of both. The user cedes control. The engineer cedes visibility. The error moves from being a suggestion to review, to an action you must now explain and undo.

Consider the feedback loop speed. A tool that suggests a code change gets corrected in the PR comment. The cost is a few seconds of review. An agent that merges a flawed change triggers a bug ticket, a rollback, a post-mortem. The cost is hours of engineering time and a breach of process. The draft paradigm keeps the cost of failure low, and the learning cycle fast.

## The Illusion of Completion

LLMs are fantastic approximators. They generate coherent, plausible output. This is also their greatest danger in production. They present a solution with the confidence of a finished product, masking the underlying uncertainty. A 95% accurate summary is a draft I can perfect. A 95% accurate action executed autonomously is a 5% error rate you own.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Engineering for the Human-in-the-Loop

Building a drafts-only system changes your engineering priorities. You're not optimizing for end-to-end latency of a full transaction. You're optimizing for the latency and quality of the first draft. This is a different, often simpler, problem.

You measure different things. Instead of just "task success rate," you track "draft acceptance rate" and "human edit distance." A low edit distance means your drafts are good. A high acceptance rate means they're useful. These metrics are clearer, more actionable, and don't blur the line between AI and human responsibility. The architecture is simpler, too. You need fewer guardrails, less redundant verification, and no complex rollback mechanisms. The human is the guardrail.

## The Speed Tradeoff That Isn't

The immediate objection is speed. "But if a human has to review everything, we lose all the efficiency!" This is short-term math. In the long run, drafts-only systems get deployed faster and improved more reliably.

You can ship a draft generator when it's 80% reliable. Shipping an autonomous agent requires 99.9%+ reliability, a much higher bar. Getting to that first deployable version takes orders of magnitude more time. Furthermore, every mistake your draft system makes becomes a clear, contextual training example. The human's correction is the perfect label. Autonomous mistakes are often messier, with blame and root causes obscured.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## Practical Implementation

How does this look in practice? The interface is key. Every output must be presented as mutable, clearly in a state of proposal. Use UI patterns that imply editing: placeholder text boxes, "suggested" tags, "apply/edit/discard" button trios. The API should return structured drafts with fields easily overridden, not execute side effects.

The mental shift is to see the AI as a brilliant, tireless, but junior colleague. It prepares the work, writes the first pass, assembles the data. You, the senior engineer, review, adjust, and approve. This is a scalable, audit-friendly, and robust collaboration pattern.

## The Path to Autonomy

This isn't a permanent stance against automation. It's the safest path to get there. A drafts-only system is the ultimate training platform for a future autonomous one. You collect a dataset of perfect human decisions on top of AI proposals. You can precisely measure the gap between draft and final decision. You can then train a verifier model, or slowly automate sub-tasks where the edit distance trends to zero.

Autonomy should be earned, not assumed. It's a privilege you grant the system after it has demonstrated consistent, verifiable performance under supervision. Start with drafts. Prove reliability. Then, and only then, consider moving the human from the center of the loop to the edge of it.
